items.title: Working from Home
items.tvi: Làm việc ở nhà
items.text:
When Hoa's company let staff work from home two days a week, she was delighted. She would save an hour of travel every day and could finally have breakfast with her children.
The first month was not as easy as she had expected. Her flat was small, so she had to work at the kitchen table. Her neighbours were building a new bathroom, and the noise made phone meetings difficult. She also noticed that she was working longer hours, because there was no clear moment when the day ended.
So Hoa made some changes. She bought a small desk and put it in the corner of the bedroom. She started every home day by getting dressed as if she were going to the office, and she turned her computer off at six o'clock exactly. On Fridays she went to a café near her flat for two hours, just to see other people.
Now, she says, home days are her most productive. "The secret," she explains, "is to treat home like an office, but not to let the office take over your home."

qs.q: Why was the first month difficult for Hoa?
qs.a: Her flat was small and noisy, and she worked too long
w: Her children were at home all day
Her company asked her to come back
qs.why: “Her flat was small… the noise made phone meetings difficult… she was working longer hours.”

qs.q: What does Hoa do at six o'clock?
qs.a: She switches off her computer
qs.why: “she turned her computer off at six o'clock exactly.”

qs.q: What is Hoa's advice?
qs.a: Keep work and home life separate
w: Work in a café every day
Don't work from home at all
qs.why: “treat home like an office, but not to let the office take over your home.”

items.title: A Message from the Sports Centre
items.tvi: Thông báo của trung tâm thể thao
items.text:
Dear members,
From Monday 3 June, the swimming pool will be closed for four weeks while we replace the old changing rooms. We know many of you swim every morning, so we have made an agreement with Riverside Hotel, which is only ten minutes' walk from here. Members can use the hotel pool free of charge between 6 and 9 a.m. Please show your membership card at the hotel reception.
All other activities, including yoga, the gym and tennis, will continue as normal. However, the car park will be smaller during the building work, so we suggest you come by bike or bus if possible.
To say sorry for the trouble, every member will receive one extra month of membership at no cost. You do not need to do anything; it will be added to your account automatically.
If you have any questions, please speak to Mai at the front desk or email info@greenpark.vn.
Thank you for your patience.
Green Park Sports Centre

qs.q: Why is the pool closing?
qs.a: The changing rooms are being rebuilt
qs.why: “closed for four weeks while we replace the old changing rooms.”

qs.q: What must members do to swim at the hotel?
qs.a: Show their membership card
qs.why: “Please show your membership card at the hotel reception.”

qs.q: How will members get their extra month?
qs.a: It will be added automatically
w: They must ask Mai at the desk
qs.why: “it will be added to your account automatically.”

items.title: The Boy Who Fixed Bicycles
items.tvi: Cậu bé sửa xe đạp
items.text:
When Tuan was twelve, his bicycle broke on the way to school. His family had no money for a new one, so he took it apart in the yard and tried to repair it himself. It took him three weekends, and he made many mistakes, but in the end it worked.
Soon his neighbours began bringing him their broken bikes. At first he did it for free, but his grandmother told him that his time had value. He started charging a small amount and saved every coin in a tin box.
By the time he was sixteen, Tuan had saved enough to rent a tiny space at the market. He painted a sign that said 'Tuan's Bikes' and worked there every afternoon after school. His teachers were worried that he would fall behind, but his marks actually improved, because he had learned to plan his time carefully.
Today Tuan is twenty-five and owns two shops. He still keeps the old tin box on his desk. "It reminds me," he says, "that every big thing starts with something small."

qs.q: Why did Tuan repair his own bicycle?
qs.a: His family couldn't afford a new one
w: He wanted to start a business
qs.why: “His family had no money for a new one.”

qs.q: What did his grandmother teach him?
qs.a: That he should be paid for his work
qs.why: “his grandmother told him that his time had value. He started charging…”

qs.q: What happened to his school marks?
qs.a: They got better
qs.why: “his marks actually improved.”

items.title: Should Students Wear Uniforms?
items.tvi: Học sinh có nên mặc đồng phục?
items.text:
Last week our school asked students what they thought about uniforms. Here are two opinions.
Linh, 15: "I'm in favour of uniforms. In the morning I don't have to think about what to wear, so I save time. Also, nobody can see whose family is rich and whose family is poor, so there is less pressure. Some people say uniforms are boring, but we can still show our personality with our bags, hair and shoes."
Khang, 16: "I disagree. Uniforms are expensive, because we have to buy them from the school shop and they don't last long. They are also uncomfortable in hot weather. I think we should be allowed to wear our own clothes, with a few simple rules, for example no very short skirts or offensive slogans. Learning how to dress well is part of growing up."
The head teacher says the school will make a decision next month after talking to parents.

qs.q: According to Linh, why do uniforms reduce pressure?
qs.a: Students can't see who is rich or poor
w: Students don't need to buy bags
qs.why: “nobody can see whose family is rich and whose family is poor, so there is less pressure.”

qs.q: What does Khang say about the price of uniforms?
qs.a: They cost a lot and wear out quickly
w: They are cheaper than normal clothes
qs.why: “Uniforms are expensive… they don't last long.”

qs.q: What will happen next?
qs.a: The school will decide after talking to parents
qs.why: “the school will make a decision next month after talking to parents.”

items.title: My First Job Interview
items.tvi: Buổi phỏng vấn xin việc đầu tiên
items.text:
I had my first job interview last Tuesday, for a part-time position at a bookshop. I was so nervous that I couldn't eat breakfast. I arrived twenty minutes early, which was a good idea, because I got lost inside the shopping centre and found the shop with only five minutes to spare.
The manager, Mrs Ha, was friendly. She asked me why I wanted the job and what books I liked. I had prepared answers to these questions, so I felt more relaxed. Then she asked me something I hadn't expected: "Tell me about a time when you made a mistake." My mind went blank for a few seconds. Then I told her about a group project at school where I forgot to send an important file, and explained how I now write everything in a planner.
At the end, she showed me around the shop and introduced me to two of the staff. Yesterday she phoned to offer me the job. She said that my answer about the mistake was the reason she chose me, because it showed I could learn from problems.

qs.q: Why was it good that the writer arrived early?
qs.a: The writer got lost before finding the shop
qs.why: “I got lost inside the shopping centre and found the shop with only five minutes to spare.”

qs.q: Which question surprised the writer?
qs.a: A question about a mistake they had made
qs.why: “she asked me something I hadn't expected: Tell me about a time when you made a mistake.”

qs.q: Why did Mrs Ha choose the writer?
qs.a: The writer showed they could learn from problems
w: The writer knew a lot about books
The writer was the first to arrive
qs.why: “it showed I could learn from problems.”

items.title: Plastic in the Sea
items.tvi: Nhựa trong biển
items.text:
Every year, millions of tonnes of plastic end up in the oceans. Much of it comes from rivers, which carry rubbish from cities to the sea. Once it is in the water, plastic does not disappear. Sunlight and waves break it into very small pieces, called microplastics, which fish and birds eat by mistake.
Scientists have found microplastics in salt, in tap water and even in the air. They are still studying what this means for human health, but many experts believe we should act now rather than wait for the results.
There are some simple things everyone can do. Carrying a reusable bottle and bag is a good start. Saying no to plastic straws and choosing products with less packaging also helps. In some cities, shops give a small discount to customers who bring their own containers.
Governments have a role too. Several countries have banned single-use plastic bags, and a few have introduced deposit schemes, where people get money back when they return bottles. In places where these schemes exist, far fewer bottles are found on beaches.

qs.q: How does much of the plastic reach the sea?
qs.a: Rivers carry it from cities
w: Ships throw it into the water
qs.why: “Much of it comes from rivers, which carry rubbish from cities to the sea.”

qs.q: What do experts think we should do about health risks?
qs.a: Act now without waiting for results
w: Wait until the studies are finished
qs.why: “many experts believe we should act now rather than wait for the results.”

qs.q: What happens where deposit schemes exist?
qs.a: There are fewer bottles on beaches
qs.why: “far fewer bottles are found on beaches.”

items.title: The Night Market Cook
items.tvi: Người nấu ăn ở chợ đêm
items.text:
Mrs Lan has sold noodle soup at the same night market for thirty years. She starts preparing at two in the afternoon, cooking the broth slowly with beef bones, onions and spices. By six o'clock, when the market opens, there is already a queue at her stall.
Many customers are regulars who have been eating there since they were children. Others are tourists who have read about her online. A food blogger wrote about her soup five years ago, and since then visitors from Korea, Australia and France have come to try it. Mrs Lan does not speak much English, but she has learned to say "spicy?" and "one more?" with a big smile.
Last year a restaurant group offered her a job as head cook in their new restaurant in the city centre. The salary was good and she would work in a modern kitchen. She refused. "At the market I can talk to my customers and see their faces when they taste the soup," she says. "In a big kitchen I would just be a name on a menu."
Her daughter now helps her at weekends and is slowly learning the recipe, which has never been written down.

qs.q: Why do many tourists visit Mrs Lan's stall?
qs.a: A blogger wrote about her soup
w: Her stall is in a hotel
qs.why: “A food blogger wrote about her soup five years ago, and since then visitors… have come.”

qs.q: Why did Mrs Lan refuse the restaurant job?
qs.a: She wanted to keep contact with her customers
qs.why: “At the market I can talk to my customers and see their faces.”

qs.q: What do we learn about the recipe?
qs.a: It exists only in Mrs Lan's memory
w: It is printed on the menu
qs.why: “the recipe, which has never been written down.”

items.title: Volunteers Wanted
items.tvi: Cần tình nguyện viên
items.text:
Are you free on Saturday mornings? Do you enjoy working with children? Sunflower Library is looking for volunteers to help with our weekend reading club.
The club is for children aged six to ten who find reading difficult. Volunteers read stories with small groups, play word games and help the children choose books to borrow. You don't need to be a teacher, but you should be patient, friendly and able to read clearly. All volunteers receive a two-hour training session before they start.
We ask volunteers to come at least twice a month for six months, because the children feel more confident when they see the same faces. Sessions run from 8.30 to 11.00, and we provide free drinks and snacks.
Last year, eighty percent of the children in the club improved their reading level by at least one grade. Many parents told us their children now read at home for fun.
To apply, fill in the form on our website before 15 August. We will invite you for a short chat, and training begins on 1 September.

qs.q: Who is the reading club for?
qs.a: Children who have problems with reading
w: Children who want to become teachers
Adults who want to learn English
qs.why: “The club is for children aged six to ten who find reading difficult.”

qs.q: Why must volunteers come regularly?
qs.a: Children feel more confident with familiar faces
w: Volunteers are paid by the month
qs.why: “the children feel more confident when they see the same faces.”

qs.q: What happens after you send the form?
qs.a: You are invited for a short conversation
w: You start working the next Saturday
You must take a reading test
qs.why: “We will invite you for a short chat.”

items.title: Learning to Drive at Forty
items.tvi: Học lái xe ở tuổi bốn mươi
items.text:
For most of my life I relied on buses, taxis and my husband to get around. I always told myself I was too nervous to drive. But when we moved to a small town where buses run only twice a day, I realised I had no choice.
My first lesson was terrible. I stopped the engine five times and drove round a roundabout twice because I was too scared to leave it. My instructor, a calm man called Duc, simply laughed and said, "Everyone does that."
What helped me most was practising in a quiet car park on Sunday mornings with my son, who had passed his test the year before. He was surprisingly patient, which was funny, since I had taught him to ride a bike years earlier.
I failed my first driving test because I forgot to check my mirror before turning. I was disappointed, but I booked another test immediately. Six weeks later I passed. Now I drive to work every day, and last month I drove my mother to the coast for her birthday. The independence is wonderful. I only wish I had started twenty years earlier.

qs.q: Why did the writer decide to learn to drive?
qs.a: Public transport in her new town was very limited
w: Her son needed a lift to school
qs.why: “we moved to a small town where buses run only twice a day.”

qs.q: Why does the writer find her son's patience funny?
qs.a: She had once taught him to ride a bike
qs.why: “which was funny, since I had taught him to ride a bike years earlier.”

qs.q: How does the writer feel now?
qs.a: She enjoys her independence but regrets starting late
w: She is still afraid of driving
qs.why: “The independence is wonderful. I only wish I had started twenty years earlier.”

items.title: Review: The Lighthouse Café
items.tvi: Nhận xét: quán cà phê Ngọn Hải Đăng
items.text:
The Lighthouse Café opened in March in an old fishing house next to the harbour. The owners have kept the original wooden walls and decorated them with old maps and photos of local fishermen, which gives the place a warm, relaxed feeling.
I visited on a Wednesday afternoon. The menu is short but interesting, with local seafood, salads and homemade cakes. I had the grilled fish with lemon rice, which was fresh and perfectly cooked, although the portion was quite small for the price. My friend's coconut cake, on the other hand, was huge and delicious.
Service was friendly but slow. We waited almost twenty minutes for our drinks, and the waiter apologised, explaining that two staff members were ill. Still, I would recommend booking a table at weekends, because the terrace with its sea view fills up quickly.
Overall, the Lighthouse Café is a lovely spot for a long, relaxed lunch rather than a quick meal. Go for the view and the cakes, and don't be in a hurry.

qs.q: What does the writer say about the grilled fish?
qs.a: It was good but too small for the price
w: It was the biggest dish on the menu
qs.why: “fresh and perfectly cooked, although the portion was quite small for the price.”

qs.q: Why was the service slow that day?
qs.a: Two staff members were ill
qs.why: “two staff members were ill.”

qs.q: Who would enjoy this café most?
qs.a: People who want a long, relaxed meal
w: People who need a quick lunch
People who want a large menu
qs.why: “a lovely spot for a long, relaxed lunch rather than a quick meal.”

items.title: My First Week as a Volunteer
items.tvi: Tuần đầu làm tình nguyện viên
items.text:
Last summer I decided to spend my holidays doing something useful, so I signed up to volunteer at an animal rescue centre outside Da Lat. I had always loved animals, but I had never looked after any except our family cat.
On my first morning, the manager, Mr Hoang, gave me a pair of old boots and a bucket. "Most of the job isn't playing with puppies," he warned me with a smile. He was right. I spent the first three days cleaning cages, washing bowls and carrying heavy bags of food. By the evening my back ached and I wondered why I had come.
Things changed on the fourth day. A farmer brought in a young dog that had been hit by a motorbike. It was frightened and wouldn't let anyone near it. Mr Hoang asked me to sit quietly beside its cage for an hour every afternoon, just reading a book aloud. At first I felt silly, but by the end of the week the dog was taking food from my hand.
I learned a lot that week. I learned that caring for animals is mostly hard, unexciting work, and that patience matters more than strength. I also learned that small things, like a familiar voice, can make a big difference to a scared animal.
I'm going back next summer, and this time I'm taking my younger brother. He thinks it will be fun. I haven't told him about the buckets yet.

qs.q: Before the summer, the writer's experience of caring for animals was
qs.a: limited to one pet at home
qs.why: “I had never looked after any except our family cat.”

qs.q: What did Mr Hoang mean when he gave the writer boots and a bucket?
qs.a: The work would be mostly dirty and practical
w: The writer would work outdoors in the rain
The writer should bring their own equipment
The centre was short of money
qs.why: “Most of the job isn't playing with puppies.” Sau đó toàn là dọn chuồng, rửa bát.

qs.q: How did the writer feel at the end of the first three days?
qs.a: Tired and unsure about the decision
qs.why: “my back ached and I wondered why I had come.”

qs.q: Why did the writer read aloud next to the dog's cage?
qs.a: To help the dog get used to a calm human voice
w: To practise for a school exam
To stop the dog from barking at night
qs.why: Đoạn 3–4: chú chó sợ người; giọng quen làm nó bình tĩnh dần (“a familiar voice”).

qs.q: The word “unexciting” in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to
qs.a: dull
qs.why: unexciting = không thú vị, đơn điệu = dull.

qs.q: What does the final sentence suggest about the writer?
qs.a: They are amused that their brother does not know about the hard work
w: They think their brother will not be allowed to go
They will not do any cleaning next time
qs.why: Câu cuối nói đùa: em trai nghĩ sẽ vui, người viết chưa kể chuyện phải xách xô dọn dẹp.

items.title: Why We Should Bring Back Paper Maps
items.tvi: Vì sao nên dùng lại bản đồ giấy
items.text:
These days, almost nobody I know carries a paper map. Why would they? A phone can show you exactly where you are, tell you which way to turn and warn you about traffic. I use one myself every day. Even so, I think we have lost something important.
When I was a teenager, my father taught me to read a map before every family trip. We would spread it across the kitchen table and plan the route together. I had to notice rivers, hills and the names of towns we would pass. As a result, I still have a clear picture in my head of how my country fits together.
Scientists have found some evidence that people who depend on step-by-step directions remember less about the places they visit. When a voice tells you to "turn left in 200 metres", you don't need to pay attention to anything else, so your brain doesn't bother building a mental map. People who use paper maps, on the other hand, have to look around and connect what they see with what is on the page.
I am not suggesting that we throw our phones away. They are fast and useful, especially in a city you don't know. But next time you go somewhere new, try looking at a map before you leave, or switch the directions off for part of the journey. You might get lost once or twice. That's fine. Getting a little lost is often how we really learn a place.

qs.q: What is the writer's attitude to phone directions?
qs.a: They are useful, but they have a disadvantage
w: They are dangerous and should be banned
They are better than paper maps in every way
They are too difficult for older people
qs.why: “I use one myself every day. Even so, I think we have lost something important.”

qs.q: What did the writer do with their father before trips?
qs.a: Planned the route on a map together
w: Drove the route the day before
Wrote down directions from a book
Asked neighbours for the best way
qs.why: “spread it across the kitchen table and plan the route together.”

qs.q: According to the article, people who follow step-by-step directions
qs.a: may remember less about places
w: arrive more quickly than map users
are more likely to have accidents
qs.why: “people who depend on step-by-step directions remember less about the places they visit.”

qs.q: Why, according to the writer, doesn't the brain build a mental map when following a voice?
qs.a: Because it does not need to pay attention to the surroundings
w: Because the voice speaks too quickly
Because phone maps are often wrong
Because people use phones only in cities
qs.why: “you don't need to pay attention to anything else, so your brain doesn't bother building a mental map.”

qs.q: What does the writer advise readers to do?
qs.a: Look at a map before a journey or turn directions off sometimes
w: Only visit places they already know
Buy a new paper map for every trip
qs.why: Đoạn cuối: “try looking at a map before you leave, or switch the directions off for part of the journey.”

qs.q: In the last paragraph, the writer suggests that getting lost
qs.a: can help people learn about a place
w: should be avoided at all costs
only happens to paper map users
is a sign of a bad phone
qs.why: “Getting a little lost is often how we really learn a place.”

items.title: Review: The Green Kitchen
items.tvi: Nhận xét: nhà hàng The Green Kitchen
items.text:
The Green Kitchen opened three months ago in a quiet street near the river, and it is already difficult to get a table at the weekend. The restaurant serves only vegetarian food, and most of the vegetables come from the owner's own farm, just forty minutes away.
I visited on a Thursday evening with two friends, one of whom usually refuses to eat any meal without meat. The menu is short, with just five main dishes, which I think is a good sign: the kitchen clearly prefers to do a few things well. We started with fresh spring rolls and a pumpkin soup that was rich and full of flavour. My meat-loving friend asked for a second bowl.
The main courses were less consistent. The mushroom curry was excellent, but the vegetable burger was dry and rather plain, and it arrived a good ten minutes after the other dishes. When we mentioned this to the waiter, he apologised and did not charge us for it, which was a nice gesture.
The dining room is simple, with wooden tables and plenty of plants, though it gets quite noisy when it is full. Prices are reasonable for the quality, and portions are generous.
Overall, The Green Kitchen is a welcome addition to the area. It isn't perfect yet, but the ingredients are excellent and the staff obviously care. If they sort out the problems with timing in the kitchen, it could become one of the best places to eat in town. Book ahead, and don't miss the soup.

qs.q: Why is it hard to get a table at the weekend?
qs.a: The restaurant has quickly become popular
w: The restaurant is only open at weekends
The owner reserves tables for farmers
qs.why: “it is already difficult to get a table at the weekend” sau 3 tháng mở cửa: quán đông khách.

qs.q: The writer thinks the short menu is
qs.a: a sign that the kitchen focuses on quality
w: a way to keep prices low
qs.why: “which I think is a good sign: the kitchen clearly prefers to do a few things well.”

qs.q: What does the writer's friend asking for a second bowl of soup show?
qs.a: Even a meat lover enjoyed the vegetarian food
w: The friend did not like the main courses
qs.why: Người bạn thường không ăn bữa nào thiếu thịt mà vẫn xin thêm súp.

qs.q: What problem did the group have?
qs.a: One dish was poor and came late
w: The waiter was rude to them
The bill was higher than expected
qs.why: “the vegetable burger was dry and rather plain, and it arrived a good ten minutes after the other dishes.”

qs.q: The phrase “a nice gesture” refers to
qs.a: not charging for the burger
w: bringing a second bowl of soup
qs.why: “he apologised and did not charge us for it, which was a nice gesture.”

qs.q: What is the writer's overall opinion?
qs.a: Good with some problems that could be fixed
qs.why: “It isn't perfect yet… If they sort out the problems with timing… it could become one of the best places.”

items.title: The Teenager Who Fixes Phones
items.tvi: Cậu thiếu niên sửa điện thoại
items.text:
Every Saturday morning, a queue forms outside a small shop in Hai Phong. People are waiting for sixteen-year-old Minh, who repairs broken phones, tablets and headphones for a fraction of what most repair shops charge.
Minh started by accident. Two years ago he dropped his own phone and cracked the screen. His parents said they could not afford a new one, so he watched online videos, ordered a replacement screen for a few dollars and fixed it himself at the kitchen table. "It took me five hours and I nearly gave up twice," he laughs. "Now I can do it in twenty minutes."
Word spread quickly. Soon friends and neighbours were bringing him their devices, and his uncle offered him a corner of his electronics shop at weekends. Minh charges only for the parts plus a small fee, and he always explains to customers what went wrong. "I want people to understand their phones," he says. "Then they won't throw them away so quickly."
That idea matters to him. Minh has read about the huge amount of electronic waste produced every year and about the people, often children, who sort through it in dangerous conditions. He believes that repairing things is one small way to reduce the problem.
His teachers are proud of him, although they admit they sometimes worry that his weekend job could affect his studies. Minh is not worried. He wants to study engineering at university, and he says that fixing phones has taught him more about electronics than any textbook.

qs.q: Why did Minh repair his own phone the first time?
qs.a: His family could not pay for a new one
w: He wanted to start a business
His uncle asked him to try
qs.why: “His parents said they could not afford a new one.”

qs.q: What does Minh's comment about five hours show?
qs.a: The first repair was difficult for him
w: He was very fast from the start
He did not enjoy the work
qs.why: “It took me five hours and I nearly gave up twice.”

qs.q: The phrase “Word spread quickly” means that
qs.a: many people soon heard about Minh's skill
w: people sent messages about broken phones
qs.why: word spread = tin lan nhanh: bạn bè, hàng xóm biết và mang máy tới.

qs.q: Why does Minh explain what went wrong to customers?
qs.a: He hopes they will keep their devices longer
w: He wants them to pay more
It is the law in Viet Nam
qs.why: “I want people to understand their phones… Then they won't throw them away so quickly.”

qs.q: What worries Minh's teachers?
qs.a: His weekend work might be bad for his schoolwork
w: He might hurt himself with tools
He wants to leave school early
qs.why: “his weekend job could affect his studies.”

qs.q: How does Minh feel about his future?
qs.a: Confident that his repair work will help him
w: Sure he will open a big repair shop
qs.why: “Minh is not worried… fixing phones has taught him more about electronics than any textbook.”

items.title: Ask Lan: My Friend Is Always Late
items.tvi: Hỏi Lan: bạn tôi luôn đến muộn
items.text:
Dear Lan,
I have a problem with my best friend, Hoa. We have known each other since primary school and I really like her, but she is always late. Last week I waited forty minutes for her outside the cinema and we missed the start of the film. When she finally arrived, she just laughed and said the traffic was terrible. It happens almost every time we meet. I don't want to lose her as a friend, but I'm getting tired of waiting. What should I do?
Thanh

Dear Thanh,
You are not alone. Many friendships have a "late one" and a "waiting one", and it can cause a lot of quiet anger. The good news is that this problem can usually be solved, as long as you talk about it.
First, choose a calm moment to tell Hoa how you feel, not while you are standing outside the cinema feeling annoyed. Explain that you value her friendship and that you are not trying to criticise her as a person. Instead, describe the effect her lateness has on you: "When I wait a long time, I feel that my time doesn't matter to you."
Second, make some practical changes. Meet in places where waiting is not unpleasant, like a café or a bookshop, rather than on a street corner. You could also agree on a "fifteen-minute rule": if she is more than fifteen minutes late, you start without her.
Finally, remember that some people find time management genuinely difficult. That doesn't make it acceptable, but it may help you feel less hurt. If Hoa cares about you, and it sounds as if she does, she will try to change.
Lan

qs.q: What happened at the cinema?
qs.a: They missed the beginning of the film
w: Hoa did not come at all
The cinema was closed because of traffic
qs.why: “I waited forty minutes… and we missed the start of the film.”

qs.q: How did Hoa react when she arrived late?
qs.a: She did not seem to take it seriously
w: She offered to pay for the tickets
qs.why: “she just laughed and said the traffic was terrible.”

qs.q: What does Lan mean by “quiet anger”?
qs.a: Bad feelings that people keep to themselves
qs.why: Người chờ thường bực mà không nói ra.

qs.q: Lan suggests Thanh should talk to Hoa
qs.a: when Thanh is not feeling annoyed
w: in a message rather than face to face
qs.why: “choose a calm moment… not while you are standing outside the cinema feeling annoyed.”

qs.q: Why does Lan recommend meeting in a café or bookshop?
qs.a: Waiting there is more pleasant
qs.why: “Meet in places where waiting is not unpleasant.”

qs.q: What is Lan's attitude in the final paragraph?
qs.a: Understanding towards Hoa but clear that lateness is a problem
w: Critical of Thanh for being impatient
Sure that Hoa does not care about Thanh
qs.why: “That doesn't make it acceptable, but it may help you feel less hurt.”

items.title: The Library That Lends Tools
items.tvi: Thư viện cho mượn dụng cụ
items.text:
Most people have a drill at home that they use for about ten minutes a year. In the town of Millbrook, a group of neighbours decided this was a waste of money and space. Two years ago they opened a 'tool library' in an empty shop on the high street.
It works like a normal library. Members pay a small fee of ten pounds a year and can borrow up to three tools at a time for one week. There are more than four hundred items, from ladders and saws to sewing machines and tents. Most of them were given by local people who no longer needed them.
The library is run by volunteers, and every Saturday morning a retired builder called Peter teaches beginners how to use the tools safely. "Some people are nervous the first time," he says. "By the end of the morning, they're putting up shelves."
Not everything has gone smoothly. In the first year, several tools came back broken, so now members must pay for repairs if something is damaged.

qs.q: Where did most of the tools come from?
qs.a: Local people gave them
w: A builder's shop sold them cheaply
qs.why: “Most of them were given by local people who no longer needed them.”

qs.q: What does Peter do on Saturday mornings?
qs.a: He shows beginners how to use tools safely
w: He collects fees from new members
qs.why: “a retired builder called Peter teaches beginners how to use the tools safely.”

qs.q: Why must members now pay for repairs?
qs.a: Some tools were returned damaged
w: The fee is too low to cover costs
Peter can no longer fix them for free
qs.why: “several tools came back broken, so now members must pay for repairs”

items.title: An Email from a Host Family
items.tvi: Thư của gia đình nhận học sinh ở nhờ
items.text:
Hi Minh,
We're really looking forward to meeting you next Saturday! Just a few things before you arrive.
Our house is about twenty minutes from the airport by car. Unfortunately, neither of us can pick you up, because Sarah works on Saturdays and I'll be at our son's football match. But don't worry – the airport bus stops right at the end of our street. Get off at Park Road, and our house is the blue one opposite the bakery.
You'll have your own room on the top floor, with a desk for studying. The internet password is on a card on the desk. We usually have dinner at half past six. Please let us know if there's anything you don't eat – Sarah is a vegetarian, so we eat a lot of vegetables anyway!
Your school is a fifteen-minute walk away. On Monday morning I'll walk there with you so you can learn the way.
See you soon,
David

qs.q: How will Minh get to the house?
qs.a: By airport bus
w: Sarah will meet him at the airport
qs.why: “the airport bus stops right at the end of our street.”

qs.q: Why does David ask about food?
qs.a: He wants to know if there is anything Minh doesn't eat
w: He wants Minh to cook one evening
He thinks Minh is a vegetarian
qs.why: “Please let us know if there's anything you don't eat”

qs.q: What will happen on Monday morning?
qs.a: David will show Minh the way to school
w: Minh will take the bus to school
qs.why: “On Monday morning I'll walk there with you so you can learn the way.”

items.title: A Week Without My Phone
items.tvi: Một tuần không có điện thoại
items.text:
Last month my phone fell into a river during a camping trip. The shop said a new one would take a week to arrive, so I had no choice: I had to live without it.
The first two days were difficult. I kept putting my hand in my pocket to check messages that weren't there. I missed a friend's party because I didn't know it had moved to a different café. And without a map on my phone, I got lost on my way to a job interview and arrived ten minutes late.
But by Wednesday, something changed. On the bus I looked out of the window instead of at a screen, and I noticed a small bookshop I had passed a hundred times. I read two novels that week – more than I'd read in the whole of the previous year. I also slept better, because I wasn't checking social media in bed.
When the new phone arrived, I was happy to have it back. But I've made one rule: it stays in the kitchen at night.

qs.q: Why did the writer arrive late for a job interview?
qs.a: Because the writer got lost
qs.why: “without a map on my phone, I got lost on my way to a job interview”

qs.q: What did the writer notice on the bus?
qs.a: A bookshop
qs.why: “I noticed a small bookshop I had passed a hundred times.”

items.title: From Rice Field to Online Shop
items.tvi: Từ ruộng lúa đến cửa hàng trên mạng
items.text:
For thirty years, Mr Tuan sold his rice to a trader who came to his village in the Mekong Delta after every harvest. The trader decided the price, and it was always low.
In 2021, Mr Tuan's daughter Linh came home from university in Can Tho with an idea. She took photos of the fields, of the family drying rice in the sun and of her father's hands holding the grain. Then she opened a small online shop and posted the photos with the story of the farm.
At first, only friends and relatives bought anything. But one video of her father explaining how he grew rice without chemicals was shared thousands of times. Within a month, they had orders from Hanoi, Da Nang and even Singapore.
Now the family sells about half of their rice online, at almost twice the old price. It isn't easy: Linh spends every evening answering messages and packing orders. "But for the first time," she says, "my father decides what his work is worth."

qs.q: What was the problem with selling rice to the trader?
qs.a: The price was always low
w: He only came every few years
He wanted rice grown without chemicals
qs.why: “The trader decided the price, and it was always low.”

qs.q: What helped the shop become popular?
qs.a: A video that many people shared
qs.why: “one video of her father… was shared thousands of times.”

items.title: Ask the Expert: Saving for a Trip
items.tvi: Hỏi chuyên gia: tiết kiệm tiền đi du lịch
items.text:
Question: I'm nineteen and I want to travel around Southeast Asia next summer, but I never have any money left at the end of the month. How can I save? – Bao
Answer: Dear Bao, first of all, find out where your money goes. For two weeks, write down everything you spend, even a coffee. Most people are surprised by how much the small things add up to.
Next, decide how much the trip will cost and divide that by the number of months until you leave. That's your monthly target. On the day you get paid, move that amount into a separate savings account straight away. Don't wait to see what's left at the end of the month, because there won't be anything!
Finally, look for cheaper ways to have fun. Cook with friends instead of eating out, and borrow books instead of buying them. Saving shouldn't mean staying at home alone every weekend.
Good luck – and send us a postcard!

qs.q: What should Bao do first?
qs.a: Write down everything he spends for two weeks
qs.why: “For two weeks, write down everything you spend, even a coffee.”

qs.q: When should Bao move money into his savings account?
qs.a: As soon as he is paid
w: At the end of each month
When he has decided where to go
qs.why: “On the day you get paid, move that amount… straight away.”

qs.q: What does the expert say about having fun?
qs.a: Bao can still enjoy himself without spending much
w: Bao should stay at home every weekend
Bao should only go out when friends pay
qs.why: “Saving shouldn't mean staying at home alone every weekend.”

items.title: Seed Swap at Oak Street
items.tvi: Đổi hạt giống ở phố Oak
items.text:
Notice to all residents
The Oak Street Community Garden will hold its first Seed Swap on Saturday 14 March, from ten o'clock until two. Do you have too many tomato seeds? Did your beans grow better than you expected? Bring a few packets and take home something different.
You do not need to be a member to join in. Please put your seeds in a small paper bag and write the name of the plant and the year on the front. Seeds older than three years may not grow well, so we cannot accept them.
There will be a table of free gardening books, and Mrs Okoye, who has grown vegetables for forty years, will answer questions at eleven. Tea and homemade cakes will be sold, and all the money will pay for new tools.
If it rains, the event will move into the church hall next door. Parking is limited, so we kindly ask you to walk or cycle if you can.
We hope to see you there!

qs.q: What must visitors do with the seeds they bring?
qs.a: Put them in a bag with a label
w: Pay a small fee for them
qs.why: “Please put your seeds in a small paper bag and write the name of the plant and the year on the front.”

qs.q: What will happen to the money from the cakes?
qs.a: It will buy new tools
w: It will pay for the church hall
qs.why: “Tea and homemade cakes will be sold, and all the money will pay for new tools.”

qs.q: Where will the event be held if the weather is bad?
qs.a: In a nearby hall
qs.why: “If it rains, the event will move into the church hall next door.”

items.title: My Year with the Guitar
items.tvi: Một năm học đàn guitar
items.text:
Last January I made a promise to myself: I would learn to play the guitar before my thirtieth birthday. I had never played any instrument, so I was not sure I could do it.
For the first month, my fingers hurt every evening. I could only play three chords, and they sounded terrible. My flatmate, Daniel, started leaving the flat whenever I practised, and I did not blame him.
Then I found a teacher called Mrs Park, who runs lessons in the local school on Wednesday nights. She told me to practise for fifteen minutes every day instead of two hours at the weekend. That small change made a big difference. By June, I could play a whole song without stopping.
Last month I played at a friend's wedding. I was so nervous that my hands shook, but nobody seemed to mind. Afterwards, an old man told me he had enjoyed it.
I still make mistakes, but I no longer feel afraid to try. Next year, I want to learn to sing as well.

qs.q: Why did Daniel often leave the flat?
qs.a: The writer's playing sounded bad
w: He had to go to his lessons
He was learning an instrument too
qs.why: “I could only play three chords, and they sounded terrible. My flatmate, Daniel, started leaving the flat whenever I practised”

qs.q: What advice did Mrs Park give?
qs.a: Practise a little every day
qs.why: “She told me to practise for fifteen minutes every day instead of two hours at the weekend.”

qs.q: How did the writer feel at the wedding?
qs.a: Very nervous
qs.why: “I was so nervous that my hands shook”

items.title: An Email to the Landlord
items.tvi: Email gửi chủ nhà
items.text:
Dear Mr Hughes,
I am writing about a problem in my flat. Since the beginning of February, there has been a loud noise from the heating system every night. It starts at about eleven o'clock and continues until morning, so I am not sleeping well.
I first told your assistant about it on 10 February. She said an engineer would visit within a week. Unfortunately, nobody has come yet, and it is now 27 February.
I understand that you are very busy, and I do not want to cause difficulties. However, I have an important exam next month, and I need to rest properly. I would be very grateful if you could arrange a visit as soon as possible. I am at home every afternoon after three, or I can leave my key with the neighbour in Flat 4.
If the problem is not solved by the end of next week, I will have to ask the housing office for advice.
Thank you for your help.
Yours sincerely,
Maria Lopes

qs.q: When does the noise happen?
qs.a: During the night
w: Every time the heating is turned off
qs.why: “It starts at about eleven o'clock and continues until morning”

qs.q: What did the assistant promise?
qs.a: That an engineer would come soon
w: That the heating would be replaced
That the rent would be lower
qs.why: “She said an engineer would visit within a week.”

qs.q: What will Maria do if nothing changes next week?
qs.a: Ask the housing office for advice
w: Speak to Mr Hughes in person
qs.why: “I will have to ask the housing office for advice.”

items.title: Repair Café Opens in Town
items.tvi: Quán sửa đồ mở trong thị trấn
items.text:
Is your toaster broken? Has your favourite jumper got a hole in it? Before you throw it away, bring it to the Repair Café!
Every second Sunday of the month, from two to five, the old town hall becomes a friendly workshop. Volunteers with years of experience in electrical work, sewing and carpentry will help you repair your things for free. You can watch and learn, or just have a chat over a cup of coffee.
The idea started in the Netherlands and has now spread to hundreds of towns. Our team believes that mending things saves money, reduces waste and brings people together.
Please remember a few points. We cannot repair mobile phones or computers. Each person may bring up to two items. Because the room is small, the first twenty visitors will be seen at three o'clock, and the rest at four.
New volunteers are always welcome. If you can fix bicycles, we need you most of all!
For more details, ask at the front desk of the library.

qs.q: How much does it cost to have something repaired?
qs.a: Nothing
qs.why: “Volunteers with years of experience in electrical work, sewing and carpentry will help you repair your things for free.”

qs.q: What can the Repair Café NOT fix?
qs.a: Computers
qs.why: “We cannot repair mobile phones or computers.”

qs.q: What kind of volunteer do they want most?
qs.a: Someone who can repair bicycles
qs.why: “If you can fix bicycles, we need you most of all!”

items.title: The Envelope on the Bus
items.tvi: Phong bì trên xe buýt
items.text:
Tomas was going home on the number 12 bus when he noticed a brown envelope under the seat in front of him. Inside, there was a pile of money and a small card with a name: Mrs Ayla Demir.
He was a student, and he had very little money that month. For a moment he thought about keeping a few notes. Then he imagined how worried the owner must feel, and he changed his mind.
There was no address on the card, but the bus driver knew a lady with that name. She lived near the last stop and often travelled to the market. Tomas walked to her street and asked two neighbours, who showed him the right door.
Mrs Demir opened it and began to cry with relief. The money was for her grandson's school trip, and she had been looking for the envelope all afternoon.
She wanted to give Tomas a reward, but he refused. In the end, he accepted a plate of her homemade cakes. He said they were the best he had ever eaten.

qs.q: What was inside the envelope?
qs.a: Money and a card
qs.why: “Inside, there was a pile of money and a small card with a name: Mrs Ayla Demir.”

qs.q: How did Tomas find the owner's home?
qs.a: The driver and neighbours helped him
w: He followed her from the market
qs.why: “the bus driver knew a lady with that name … Tomas walked to her street and asked two neighbours”

qs.q: What did Tomas accept from Mrs Demir?
qs.a: Some home-made food
qs.why: “In the end, he accepted a plate of her homemade cakes.”

items.title: Interview: The Baker Who Starts at Four
items.tvi: Phỏng vấn: người thợ bánh dậy lúc bốn giờ
items.text:
We spoke to Rosa Martin, who owns a small bakery in the old part of the city.
Interviewer: What time does your day start?
Rosa: At four in the morning. The bread has to be ready before the shops open at seven, so there is no time to waste.
Interviewer: That sounds tiring. Why do you do it?
Rosa: My grandfather had a bakery, and I used to help him as a child. The smell of fresh bread reminds me of him. I tried office work for three years, but I was never happy.
Interviewer: What is the hardest part?
Rosa: Not the early mornings, actually. It is the cost of flour and electricity. Prices have gone up, but I do not want to charge my customers too much.
Interviewer: What would you tell young people who want to start a business?
Rosa: Be patient. For the first year, I earned almost nothing. Now I have six workers and a queue outside every morning. Good things take time.

qs.q: Why must Rosa start work so early?
qs.a: The bread must be ready for the morning
w: She has to meet her workers
qs.why: “The bread has to be ready before the shops open at seven”

qs.q: What does Rosa find most difficult?
qs.a: The rising costs
qs.why: “It is the cost of flour and electricity. Prices have gone up”

qs.q: What happened in her first year?
qs.a: She made very little money
qs.why: “For the first year, I earned almost nothing.”

items.title: Why I Walk to School
items.tvi: Vì sao tôi đi bộ đến trường
items.text:
Every morning, my mother offers to drive me to school, and every morning I say no. Some of my classmates think I am strange, but I have good reasons.
First, the walk takes twenty-five minutes, which is just enough time to wake up properly. By the time I arrive, my head is clear and I feel ready to learn. When I go by car, I often fall asleep in the back seat.
Second, I have a chance to listen to music or podcasts without anybody talking to me. It is the only quiet time in my busy day.
Third, walking is good for the environment. There are already too many cars outside the school gates at eight o'clock, and the air smells terrible.
Of course, it is not perfect. In winter, my shoes get wet, and sometimes I am late if I stop to talk to friends. But I would rather walk in the rain than sit in traffic.
So, if you live less than two miles away, why not try it for a week?

qs.q: What happens when the writer goes by car?
qs.a: He sometimes sleeps
qs.why: “When I go by car, I often fall asleep in the back seat.”

qs.q: What is the writer's second reason?
qs.a: He enjoys time alone
qs.why: “I have a chance to listen to music or podcasts without anybody talking to me.”

qs.q: What is a problem with walking in winter?
qs.a: His shoes become wet
qs.why: “In winter, my shoes get wet”

items.title: Change of Plan for the Class Trip
items.tvi: Thay đổi kế hoạch chuyến đi của lớp
items.text:
Dear parents and students,
I am sorry to tell you that next Friday's trip to the Science Museum has been cancelled. The coach company called this morning to say that one of their drivers is ill and they have no other driver available.
We have decided not to look for a new company. The museum is a long way from school, and a late booking would cost almost twice as much. Instead, we will invite a scientist from the local university to visit the school on the same day.
The visit will begin at nine thirty in the main hall. Students will take part in three experiments and have time to ask questions. Please bring a notebook and a pen. School uniform is not necessary, but old clothes are a good idea because one experiment can be messy.
The money you have already paid will be returned to your child's account within ten days.
We will try to organise the museum trip again in the spring.
Kind regards,
Mr Collins

qs.q: Why was the trip cancelled?
qs.a: The coach had no driver
qs.why: “one of their drivers is ill and they have no other driver available.”

qs.q: What will happen on Friday instead?
qs.a: A scientist will visit the school
w: Students will go to the university
qs.why: “we will invite a scientist from the local university to visit the school on the same day.”

qs.q: Why should students wear old clothes?
qs.a: An experiment may be messy
qs.why: “old clothes are a good idea because one experiment can be messy.”

items.title: Bees in the City
items.tvi: Ong trong thành phố
items.text:
Many people think that bees live only in the countryside, but more and more of them now live on the roofs of city buildings. In some cities, hotels, banks and even theatres keep hives, and the honey is sold in their shops.
City bees often do better than country bees. In the countryside, farmers use strong chemicals to protect their crops, and these can harm bees. In towns, there are fewer chemicals and a great variety of flowers in parks and gardens, so the bees can find food nearly all year.
Keeping bees is not difficult, but it takes patience. A beginner needs a special suit, a small hive and about two hours a week. Many cities now offer courses for new beekeepers.
However, experts warn that too many hives can be a problem. If there are not enough flowers, the bees may have to fight for food, and wild insects can suffer.
The best way to help, they say, is simple: plant more flowers on balconies and in gardens, and avoid chemicals.

qs.q: Why do city bees often do well?
qs.a: There are fewer harmful chemicals
w: There are no flowers in towns
qs.why: “In towns, there are fewer chemicals and a great variety of flowers in parks and gardens”

qs.q: What does a beginner need?
qs.a: Some equipment and a little time
qs.why: “A beginner needs a special suit, a small hive and about two hours a week.”

qs.q: What is the experts' main warning?
qs.a: Too many hives may cause trouble
w: Honey is not safe to eat
qs.why: “too many hives can be a problem. If there are not enough flowers, the bees may have to fight for food”
